design_detail: Open, uncontrolled before-and-after challenge study in 6 men who had used amphetamines recreationally. Each took 10 mg of slow-release oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn Gradumet) at 9 a.m. in the laboratory on 13 consecutive days (days 2-14). On day 1, before the daily dosing began, and on day 15, after it ended, each received an oral challenge dose of deuterated methamphetamine 0.125 mg/kg, so that the plasma concentrations from the challenge could be told apart from those left by the daily dosing. Heart rate, blood pressure, a 0-100 self-rating of 'high' and plasma concentrations of both forms were measured on the two challenge days, with blood sampled to 48 hours. No placebo, no randomization and no blinding are described.
can_establish: Whether the heart-rate, blood-pressure, subjective and pharmacokinetic responses to one low oral dose of methamphetamine differ after thirteen days of daily low-dose exposure, within the same six men.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance develops to subjective effects at doses large enough to produce them (the challenge produced a mean peak 'high' below 20 out of 100) or to blood-pressure effects (peak rises were under 15 mm Hg systolic), both of which the authors state the study could not test; anything about the doses, routes or binge patterns of non-medical use; and whether the heart-rate change reflects tolerance rather than habituation to the laboratory, since there was no placebo condition and no control group.

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; the recruitment route is not described (p. 353).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy men who had previously used amphetamines for recreational purposes, selected for infrequent past use so that tolerance would have room to develop; each agreed to abstain from amphetamines and any other illegal drug for two weeks before and throughout the study, with daily urine screening. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria are listed (pp. 353-354).
sample.demographics: Six men, age 24 years (SEM 2), weight 72.6 kg (SEM 1.1), height 179 cm (SEM 3.6); lifetime use of amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or methamphetamine 8 times (SEM 3.9) (p. 353).
sample.attrition: None reported; six men are described throughout.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, healthy, with a lifetime average of about eight occasions of amphetamine use; a sample chosen for low previous exposure so that tolerance could develop, and far from the pattern of people who use methamphetamine heavily.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory each morning and measured directly in plasma: gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with a deuterated internal standard quantified deuterated (challenge) and non-deuterated (daily-dose) methamphetamine separately, with blood drawn every 30 minutes for the first 4 hours and at 5, 6, 8, 10, 24, 28, 32 and 48 hours (pp. 354-355).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 10 mg of a slow-release oral preparation each morning for 13 consecutive days, with oral challenge doses of deuterated methamphetamine 0.125 mg/kg on day 1 and day 15. The authors state the daily dose was chosen as a commonly used therapeutic dose that in pilot work caused no adverse effect other than falling asleep earlier than usual (pp. 353-354).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants contracted to abstain from amphetamines and any other illegal drug for two weeks before and throughout the study; daily urine samples tested by EMIT were consistently negative. Tobacco, alcohol and caffeine are not mentioned (p. 353).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks' abstinence before the study and throughout, verified by daily urine screening. On day 15 the challenge was given on top of residual drug from the daily dosing: non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 5.03 ng/mL (SEM 1.88) before the challenge dose (pp. 353, 355).

comparison.controls: The same six men on day 1, before the daily dosing began; there was no placebo condition and no separate control group.
comparison.matching: Within-person before-and-after comparison; the order is fixed by the design (day 1 always precedes day 15), so period and order effects cannot be separated from drug effects.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person comparison, but nothing controls for repetition: familiarity with the procedure, the room and the measurements can lower a cardiovascular response on a second occasion, and no placebo challenge was run to measure that.

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate from a chest-electrode electrocardiogram and blood pressure from an automated portable monitor (Accutracker), analysed only at baseline and at 2.5 and 3.5 hours after dosing because psychomotor testing contaminated the other time points; a 0-100 self-rating of 'high' anchored at 100 to the highest the person had ever been on amphetamines, repeated at frequent intervals, with each rating made while the person was shown his previous rating; plasma concentrations by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. A neuropsychological battery was given but reported elsewhere (pp. 354-355).
outcomes.validity_norms: The 'high' scale is anchored to each person's own previous experience rather than to a common standard, so ratings are not comparable between people; cardiovascular measurement is objective.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a smaller rise in heart rate over baseline on day 15 than on day 1 at the two uncontaminated time points.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described; repeated-measures analyses of variance were run on heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, ratings of 'high' and plasma concentrations, and the report states that no other cardiovascular effect reached significance (p. 355).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the study was open, with no placebo condition, and both participants and investigators knew which day was which.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes, confidence intervals or printed means for the cardiovascular outcome: the heart-rate result is given as F=8.26 with P below 0.035 in the summary and P below 0.03 in the Results, and the day-1 and day-15 rises are shown only as bars in Figure 3 (about 10 and 7 beats/min at 2.5 h and about 14 and 8 beats/min at 3.5 h, read from the figure and not printed). Peak 'high' was 16.8 (SEM 6.5) of 100 on day 1 and 10.0 (SEM 3.9) on day 15, a difference the authors report as not significant; peak plasma concentrations occurred at 3.1 h (SEM 0.3) and 2.8 h (SEM 0.4) and did not differ. Converting the standard errors with six participants gives standard deviations of about 15.9 and 9.6 for the two 'high' ratings (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures analyses of variance on the raw measures.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the consent form was approved by the University of North Carolina committee for the protection of human subjects (p. 353).
analysis.selective_reporting: The neuropsychological battery, named in the introduction as part of the study, is deferred to a separate report; blood-pressure results are given only as the statement that systolic pressure rose over time on both days with no other significant effect; the time course of 'high' is not shown at all.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With six men and a within-person comparison the heart-rate test has F(1,5), and the authors state explicitly that the small subjective and blood-pressure responses to the challenge dose limited the chance of observing tolerance in those measures.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After thirteen days of 10 mg a day, the same challenge dose produced a smaller rise in heart rate than before (F=8.26, P<0.035 in the summary and P<0.03 in the Results), while peak ratings of 'high' (16.8 against 10.0 out of 100) and the plasma concentration-time course of the challenge dose were statistically unchanged. Steady-state concentrations of the daily drug were present on day 15 (5.03 ng/mL, SEM 1.88, before the challenge), so the smaller heart-rate response occurred despite a higher total drug concentration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and discussion conclude that tolerance to the cardioacceleratory effect was induced while disposition and subjective effects were unaltered, and that the reduction 'becomes more robust' once the residual drug is taken into account. The direction is supported, but with six men, no placebo and no blinding, and a single statistic, a smaller second response cannot be separated from habituation to a repeated laboratory procedure; the authors are careful to say that tolerance to the subjective and blood-pressure effects cannot be shown here because the responses were too small, which is a statement about power rather than evidence of no tolerance.

timeline.event: The pharmacokinetic arm of the same programme, in 8 men including these 6: no change in absorption, clearance or half-life after the 13-day regimen, so the heart-rate tolerance could not be explained by a change in disposition
Three days of twice-daily oral methamphetamine in a residential laboratory: tolerance to positive subjective ratings and to sleep disruption, with no fall in the anorectic effect
Repeated oral methamphetamine with and without alcohol: heart-rate increases diminished by the third administration over two days

replication.where_it_stands: A fall in the heart-rate response with repeated low oral dosing has been seen here and, over a much shorter interval, in the methamphetamine-alcohol study of Kirkpatrick and colleagues; the finding of unchanged subjective effects is specific to this study's single daily slow-release dose and small response, and the later twice-daily study found the opposite for ratings of 'high'.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse contract 271-87-8126 (p. 358).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: University of North Carolina Department of Psychiatry with Research Triangle Institute; the same investigators published the pharmacokinetic analysis of the same participants (Cook et al., 1992), so the two papers are one study reported twice and are not independent.

what_would_settle_it: The same 13-day design with a placebo challenge arm and a randomized or counterbalanced order, in a larger sample including women, at a dose that produces a substantial subjective response, so that a smaller second response can be separated from habituation and so that tolerance to the wanted effects can actually be tested.

domains.domain: Randomization process (no randomization: fixed before-and-after order)
domains.note: Day 1 always came before day 15 and there was no placebo challenge, so the comparison is a repeated measurement in a fixed order rather than an allocated comparison.

domains.domain: Period and carryover effects (within-person before and after)
domains.note: The day-15 challenge was given on top of steady-state drug from the daily dosing (5.03 ng/mL, SEM 1.88), and familiarity with the laboratory procedure on the second occasion is not controlled; the authors argue the residual drug makes the finding stronger, but it also means the two sessions are not comparable.
Open study: participants and investigators knew the order of the sessions, and the subjective rating required each person to compare himself with his own previous rating.
All six men completed both challenge sessions; no missing data are reported.

Heart rate and blood pressure were measured by instrument, and plasma concentrations by a validated assay; only two cardiovascular time points were analysable because psychomotor testing contaminated the rest, and the 'high' scale is anchored to each person's own experience.

No protocol; the neuropsychological battery is deferred to another paper; blood-pressure and subjective time courses are not printed; and the same heart-rate test is given with two different P values in the same article.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is an open before-and-after study without a placebo condition, in six men, with a single significant test to support its conclusion; the direction may well be right, and the pharmacokinetic arm rules out a disposition explanation, but the design cannot separate tolerance from habituation to a repeated procedure. The source can be cited for the observation that the heart-rate rise to a fixed oral challenge was smaller after thirteen days of daily dosing, and for the pharmacokinetic and subjective measures being unchanged in this low-response setting; it cannot be cited for the absence of tolerance to subjective effects, which the authors themselves say the study could not test.

key_findings.finding: The rise in heart rate over baseline after the same oral challenge dose was significantly smaller on day 15, after thirteen days of daily methamphetamine, than on day 1 (F=8.26, P<0.03), measured at the two time points free of psychomotor-task contamination, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after dosing.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, continuing on p. 357 above the Discussion; Figure 3 (p. 357)
key_findings.note: The summary on p. 352 prints the same test as P<0.035 and the Results as P<0.03; the day-1 and day-15 rises themselves are shown only as bars in Figure 3 and are not printed anywhere.

key_findings.finding: Heart rate rose significantly over time after the challenge on both test days (F=14.24, P<0.001) and systolic blood pressure also rose on both days (F=10.6, P<0.001); no other cardiovascular measure reached significance, and baseline heart rate and blood pressures did not differ between day 1 and day 15.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (p. 355) continuing at the top of p. 357
key_findings.note: Degrees of freedom are not given for these two tests; with six men they cannot be checked against the printed P values.

key_findings.finding: Ratings of 'high' after the challenge dose were modest and did not differ significantly between test days: mean peak 16.8 (SEM 6.5) of 100 on day 1 and 10.0 (SEM 3.9) on day 15. The authors state that this small response (under 20% of the highest the men had ever felt) limited the study's ability to observe tolerance to the subjective effect.

The disposition of the challenge dose was unchanged: plasma concentration-time curves for the deuterated drug did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15, and peak concentrations occurred at 3.1 h (SEM 0.3) and 2.8 h (SEM 0.4).
key_findings.locator: Results > Methamphetamine plasma concentrations, 1st paragraph (p. 355); Figure 1 (p. 356)

key_findings.finding: Daily dosing produced a steady state: before the day-15 challenge, non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 5.03 ng/mL (SEM 1.88), stayed about level for the next 4 hours, then declined, and was undetectable 48 hours later. Amphetamine, the metabolite, stayed below 2 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results > Methamphetamine plasma concentrations, 2nd paragraph (p. 355); Figure 2 (p. 356)

key_findings.finding: Over the thirteen days of daily dosing the men reported no 'high', no loss of appetite and no insomnia; the only effect reported was falling asleep earlier than usual, and no withdrawal symptoms or other effects were reported when dosing stopped.

Peak rises in blood pressure after the challenge were small: under 15 mm Hg systolic and under 6 mm Hg diastolic. The authors conclude that tolerance to the blood-pressure effects cannot be shown from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The same heart-rate test is printed with two different significance levels: the summary gives F(1,5)=8.26, P<=0.035 and the Results give F=8.26, P<0.03. With 1 and 5 degrees of freedom, F=8.26 corresponds to P=0.035 (editors' calculation), so the Results value is too small.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's single supporting statistic is reported inconsistently; the correct value, 0.035, is the one in the summary, and it is above the conventional 0.01 but below 0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: Degrees of freedom are given only for the heart-rate comparison (1,5). The two time-course tests (F=14.24 and F=10.6, both P<0.001) are printed without degrees of freedom, and with six men neither P value can be reproduced from a one-way within-person test: F(1,5)=14.24 gives P=0.013 and F(2,10)=14.24 gives P=0.0012 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot tell which test was run; the P<0.001 values are only reproducible if the time factor had more than two levels, which the methods (baseline, 2.5 h and 3.5 h) would allow.

reporting_issues.issue: No means, standard deviations or confidence intervals are printed for the study's main outcome. The day-1 and day-15 heart-rate rises appear only as bars with error bars in Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the tolerance cannot be quoted from the paper; any figure read off the bars would be an estimate from an image and should not be cited as a measured value.

reporting_issues.issue: Because of psychomotor testing between measurements, only baseline and the 2.5-hour and 3.5-hour time points were analysed for the cardiovascular outcome, which the methods state plainly but the summary and discussion do not repeat.
reporting_issues.consequence: The heart-rate conclusion rests on two post-dose time points chosen for being free of activity, not on the whole time course, and peak cardiovascular effects may not have been captured.

reporting_issues.issue: The challenge dose is described as '10 mg of oral deuterated methamphetamine HCl' in the summary and as '0.125 mg/kg of deuterated methamphetamine HCl' in the methods; at the mean weight of 72.6 kg these correspond to about 9.1 mg, so the summary rounds a weight-adjusted dose to a fixed one.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but a reader comparing this challenge with the 10 mg daily dose would take them to be identical when the challenge was scaled to body weight.

reporting_issues.issue: The neuropsychological battery is named in the introduction as part of the study and its results are deferred to a separate report that is not identified.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cognitive outcomes after thirteen days of daily dosing cannot be checked against the subjective and cardiovascular findings.
